CHAPTER 1 
ANALYSIS OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2026-27) 
 The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) formulates and conducts India’s foreign 
policy within the framework of our values and principles of fostering international 
peace and cooperation with the overall objective of meeting India’s strategic aims 
and aspirations as well as to secure our national interests. In pursuance of its 
mandated objectives, the MEA headquarters in New Delhi is assisted by 231 
Missions and Posts abroad, its Branch Secretariats and 37 Passport Offices in India, 
and autonomous bodies funded by it. The Ministry is also supported by other 
Ministries and State Governments which also contribute to India’s international 
engagement in consultation and coordination with MEA. 
1.2 Under the Constitution of India [Article 113 (2)], estimates of expenditure is 
submitted to Lok Sabha in the form of Demands for Grants. The Demands for Grants 
of the Ministry of External Affairs (Demand No. 29) was laid on the table of the House 
on 12 February 2026.

1.6 Regarding the percentage of GDP allocated to MEA during the last ten years, 
the Ministry responded that budget allocation as % of GDP is not maintained in the 
Ministry.  
1.7 Over the issue of MEA’s percentage allocation to GOI’s budget, the Foreign 
Secretary during testimony made the following submission on 23 February, 2026: 
“The Hon’ble Committee has also underlined the need for greater budgetary 
allocation, underscoring the decreasing share of the MEA’s allocation as a 
percentage of the overall GOI Budget. Our Budget for Financial Year 2026-27 
represents roughly 0.41 per cent of the total Union Budget, which is roughly 
the same as 2025-26. We should also note that even as our BE allocation has 
been steadily increasing over the years, so has the Budget of the 
Government. Even though our proportion remains at a constant figure, our 
actual allocations are increasing, and this is what has enabled us to meet our 
international obligations more effectively.” 
 
1.8 When asked to compare with corresponding ratios for select major countries 
with comparable global engagements, the Ministry submitted that MEA’s BE 2026-27 
is Rs 22,118.97 crore, representing roughly 0.41% of the total Union Budget. As a 
percentage of GDP, this allocation is around 0.06% based on the estimated GDP of 
approx. Rs 342 lakh crore for FY 2025-26 (actual figures not yet finalized). Official 
percentage to GDP data of major countries is not available in public domain. 
Secondary data from other sources such as research institutes and think tanks have 
observed that countries like US, UK, Singapore, Germany, France are allocating 
foreign affairs budget in the range 0.15 - 0.30% of their GDPs. It may be noted that 
fiscal years, budget categorizations and data availability vary therefore, this is also 
indicative. In FY 2025-26, the US’s International Affairs Budget is US $ 56.8 billion 
(approx. Rs 4.71 lakh Crore) while UK’s foreign, commonwealth and development 
office’s budget allocation for FY 2025-26 is around US $ 15.5 billion (approx. Rs 1.29 
lakh crore).

1.13 Responding to this query during evidence on 23 February 2026, the Foreign 
Secretary stated as under: 
“Sir, the Hon’ble Committee is already aware that we have, in the past years, 
also had provisioning amounts reflected in our Budget. Last year’s Budget did 
not have a reflection of this. The provisioning amount is an expenditure that is 
charged to the Guaranteed Redemption Fund, which is a notional expenditure 
and an adjustment of accounts between different branches of Government. 
As per the directions of the Reserve Bank of India and the Ministry of Finance, 
the MEA is required to provide from its Budget the payments that are due to 
EXIM Bank of India in lieu of what they are due to receive against the lines of 
credit that they have extended to foreign countries at our recommendation. 
The recommendation of the hon. Committee that the provisioning for non-
performing loans be allocated outside the regular MEA Budget is important. 
We will ensure that our core responsibilities are highlighted and receive 
adequate funding. We remain engaged with the RBI and the Ministry of 
Finance on this issue.” 
1.14 In its Fifth Report on DFG 2025-26, the Committee had recommended a 
budgetary enhancement of ‘at least 20 % in this fiscal year to meet the expanding 
needs and ensure more effective engagement on the global stage’. The Committee 
enquired whether the issue was taken up with the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry 
responded that in line with Hon’ble Committee’s recommendation, the matter was 
formally (vide a letter) brought to the notice of Ministry of Finance by the Foreign 
Secretary before the pre-budget meetings held for deciding RE 2025-26 and BE 
2026-27 allocations. As a result, the Ministry’s BE allocation for FY 2026-27 has been 
increased by 7.81 % over BE 2025-26.   
1.15 As regard to the adequacy of the allocated budget for the financial year to 
meet the expanding mandate and increasing global role of the Ministry of External 
Affairs (MEA), the Ministry stated that anticipation of expenditure progress in the 
fiscal year is regularly assessed, which makes budgetary demand and allocation a 
dynamic process. Instruments for re-appropriating money, such as Supplementary 
requests, permit re-prioritization and re-allocation of funds in order to allocate 
budgetary resources fully and effectively. Therefore, funding provided to the Ministry 
in BE 2026–27 reflects a fair evaluation of our current international obligations, 
predicted spending growth, and realistic assessment of requirements. The quarterly 
budgetary and spending evaluations put in place by the Ministry in the form of

budgetary distribution with a preference towards the Ministry's development 
partnership portfolio. For FY 2026-27, additional allocations, if required will be

1.16 Explicating the key factors that contributed to the upward revision in RE 
allocations during 2025-26, the Ministry stated that the upward revision in RE 
allocations is majorly attributed to Contingency Advance taken to cater to India’s

increase in developmental assistance offered to Mauritius (including budgetary 
support), Maldives and Nepal, increase in establishment expenditure in Headquarters

spending at the end of three quarters. By end-January 2026, MEA has spent more 
than 76% of the revised allocation (which is 1226.13 crore more than BE). MEA 
therefore is on track to fully utilize its budget by end of the current Financial Year.

1.21 When asked about the main budgetary constraints being faced by the MEA, 
and areas that are underfunded, the latter responded that budgetary demand and 
allocation is a dynamic exercise aided by regular assessment of Ministry’s 
expectation of expenditure progress in a given financial year. Instruments of re-

1.22 Moreover, Divisions/Spending Units accordingly make all efforts to ensure 
evenly paced expenditure, considering the constraint of Ministry’s spending being in

security, administrative, legal & economic ecosystems and varying project 
development and implementation schedules, posing significant challenge for 
alignment of expenditure to our own budget cycle. Ministry’s budgetary & expenditure 
management thus is unlike any other Ministry in Government, with global diversity of 
various ecosystems, in which our projects are executed & expenditure managed.

1.23 As India’s diplomatic presence expands globally with the opening of new 
Missions/Posts, besides the development assistance portfolio, the Ministry’s 
establishment expenditure is expected to rise as will the capital expenditure relating 
to acquisition/construction of suitable properties to house the Chanceries and 
residences.    
 
1.24 In pursuance of the Committee’s persistent recommendation, the Research 
and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) has examined empirical 
trends in MEA Budget through an inter-Ministerial comparison and cross-country 
comparison of different countries in their Report titled ‘Analysis of Trends of MEA 
Budgetary Allocation”. The Committee were keen to know whether the Ministry has 
utilized the RIS Report to advocate for a higher budgetary allocation in line with 
India’s growing global profile and activities. The Ministry stated that in accordance 
with the findings of the report, the Ministry continues to make efforts to reduce the 
gap between demand and allocation by rationalizing demand to make it more 
realistic, need-based, and aligned to targets, as recommended by the Hon’ble 
Committee, and by working more closely with the Ministry of Finance to facilitate a 
better appreciation by the latter of MEA’s important initiatives and associated funds 
requirements.    
 
1.25 On Committee’s specific incorporation of the dimension of gender budgeting in 
proposing the budgetary demands, the Ministry responded affirmatively and stated 
that it has constituted a gender budget cell, which has been tasked with 
assessing/evaluating gender related contributions of projects/schemes implemented 
by the Ministry and has been making efforts to make development assistance 
projects more gender impactful. Accordingly, Ministry has urged the relevant 
stakeholders, including the Exim Bank, to factor in gender aspects before the

India's diaspora, numbering over 32 million, constitutes one of the largest and 
most vibrant diasporic communities in the world, spread across more than 190 
countries and contributing significantly to the social, economic, and cultural fabric of 
their host nations while maintaining deep and enduring ties with the motherland. 
Consequent upon the merger of the erstwhile Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs 
(MOIA) with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) in 2016 the following Divisions 
within the MEA handles matters relating to Diaspora, their welfare and emigration” 
(i) Diaspora Engagement (DE) Division: This Division deals with matters 
relating to students and NRI marital disputes issues along with 
programmes related with engagement of Diaspora which includes Know 
India Programme (KIP), Scholarship Programme for Diaspora Children 
(SPDC), Promotion of Cultural Ties with Diaspora (PCTD), celebration of 
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) etc.  
(ii) Emigration Policy & Welfare (EP & W) Division: This Division deals with 
matters relating to Migration and Mobility including MMPAs & LMAs, 
Emigration Bill, India-EU CAMM, Global Compact on Migration, ADD, 
IMRF and other Regional Processes along with welfare initiatives for 
Indian workers abroad like PDOT, PBBY, ICWF & PKVY.  
(iii) Overseas Employment & Protector General of Emigrants (OE & PGE) 
Division: This Division deals with matters related to overseas employment 
of Indian workers, appointment of overseas recruitment agents, providing 
assistance through Pravasi Bharatiya  Sahatya Kendra (PBSK), working of 
E-Migrate Portal, Welfare measures to protect the interests of Emigrants 
working abroad etc.  
(iv) Passport Seva Programme (PSP) Division: The PSP Division of the 
Ministry provides passport services through the Central Passport 
Organization (CPO) and its network of Passport Offices, Passport Seva 
Kendras (PSKs); and Post Office Passport Seva Kendras (POPSKs).

2.18 When asked about an overview of the grievance redressal mechanisms 
available for the Indian diaspora, the Ministry stated that India has one of the largest 
and most geographically dispersed diasporas in the world. With increasing overseas 
mobility for employment, education, business and tourism, Indian Missions and Posts

transparent and time-bound manner, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) launched 
an online Consular Grievance Management System, MADAD, in February 2015 as 
part of the Government’s good governance and digital service delivery initiatives. 
2.19 The MADAD Portal provides a single, centralized platform for Indian nationals 
abroad to register, track and monitor grievances related to consular services. All 
Indian Missions and Posts abroad, along with MEA Branch Secretariats in Chennai, 
Guwahati, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Mumbai, are integrated with the portal for 
grievance redressal and follow-up. The system allows real-time monitoring, 
automated escalation, priority marking and regular status updates, thereby 
strengthening accountability and responsiveness in consular service delivery.

addressing complaints from the diaspora, the Ministry stated that over the years, the 
MADAD Portal has emerged as a key instrument for extending assistance to Indians

improved accessibility and outreach. Data from the MADAD Portal indicates that from

procedures for handling of consular grievances, through online forwarding, tracking 
and escalation until their eventual resolution. It allows direct registration of the 
grievances by the members of the public and effective tracking of the entire

III. EMIGRATION 
2.35 In recent times, international migration has assumed a pivotal role, shaped by 
demographic shifts and technological progress, significantly impacting labour 
markets worldwide. India is a leading country in the international migration dynamics 
and is advantageously poised due to its demographic potential. The emigration of 
Indian workers, particularly low-skilled and semi-skilled workers proceeding to the 
nineteen notified Emigration Check Required (ECR) countries of the Gulf, South-East 
Asia, and beyond, represents one of the most consequential and most vulnerable 
dimensions of India’s external engagement. The primary legal framework governing 
their emigration is the Emigration Act, 1983. 
Protector of Emigrants 
2.36 With the help of 16 offices of the Protector of Emigrants (POEs) located at 
Mumbai, Chennai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Kochi, 
Thiruvananthapuram, Jaipur, Lucknow, Patna, Bengaluru, Guwahati, Ranchi, 
Bhubaneswar and Agartala, the Protector General of Emigrants (PGE) enforces the 
Emigration Act, 1983. The Protectors of Emigrants performs functions assigned to 
them by this Act under the general superintendence and control of the Protector 
General of Emigrants. The main function of the Protector of Emigrants includes the 
grant of Emigration Clearance to the emigrants to ECR (Emigration Check Required) 
Countries as per the procedure prescribed under the Emigration Act, 1983, 
monitoring of recruitment process and reporting illegal agents, inspection of office 
premises of prospective Recruiting Agents (RAs) as they apply for the Registration 
Certificate and helping the Protector General of Emigrants in implementation of 
Emigration Act, 1983. As per the Act, the Recruiting Agents (RAs) are required to 
obtain Registration Certificate (RC) from the PGE before they could engage in 
recruitment for overseas employment. Emigration of ECR passport holders is 
regulated by way of grant of Emigration Clearance (EC) by any of the above 16 
officers of the POEs for employment in any of the 19 notified ECR countries, namely, 
Afghanistan, Bahrain, Indonesia, Iraq, Iran, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, 

39 | P a g e 
 
Malaysia, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Thailand, United 
Arab Emirates and Yemen. 
2.37 The mandate and core responsibilities of the Protector of Emigrants are 
defined under the Emigration Act, 1983. These duties of PoEs have been elaborated 
under Section 4 of the ibid act, as "General duties of Protectors of Emigrants—
Subject to the other provisions of this Act, every Protector of Emigrants shall, in 
addition to the special duties assigned to him by or under this Act —  
(a) protect and aid with his advice all intending emigrants and emigrants;  
(b) cause, so far as he can, all the provisions of this Act and of the rules made 
thereunder to be complied with;  
(c) inspect, to such extent and in such manner as may be prescribed— 
(i) any emigrant conveyance, or 
(ii) any other conveyance if he has reason to believe that any intending 
emigrants or emigrants are proceeding from, or returning to, India to or from a 
place outside India by such other conveyance; 
(d) aid and advise, so far as he reasonably can, emigrants who have returned to 
India. 
2.38 Apart from above duties following responsibilities have been entrusted to the 
Protector of Emigrants: 
a. Emigration Clearance: Granting Emigration Clearance (EC) to individuals 
intending to go abroad for employment to notified ECR countries, ensuring that 
applications are thoroughly verified and meet all legal requirements. 
b. Guidance and Protection: Providing comprehensive protection and guidance to 
prospective emigrants and those already deployed abroad. This includes 
rendering timely and effective advice and assistance throughout their journey and 
employment abroad. 
c. Regulatory Compliance: Ensuring all stakeholders, including Recruiting Agents 
(RAs), comply with the Emigration Act, 1983, and relevant regulations, thereby 
maintaining the integrity of the emigration system. 

40 | P a g e 
 
d. Grievance Redressal: Addressing grievances from emigrants regarding 
repatriation, employment disputes, and related issues, ensuring quick resolution 
and support. 
e. Coordination with Authorities: Engaging with the Bureau of Immigration, State 
Police, Indian Embassies, and Consulates, as well as other relevant government 
agencies, to protect emigrant welfare and enforce compliance. 
f. Monitoring and Investigation: Conducting thorough investigations into the 
treatment of emigrants, both during transit and their stay abroad, and taking 
corrective actions if required. 
g. Educational and Outreach Programs: Organizing educational initiatives and 
outreach programs to inform and educate emigrants and stakeholders about safe 
and legal migration practices. Pre-departure Orientation Training for emigrants is 
an important initiative in this direction.  
h. Policy Implementation and Feedback: Implementing policy changes and 
providing feedback to the PGE Division and Ministry of External Affairs to 
continuously enhance emigration processes and safeguard emigrant interests.

comments to the concerned Protector of Emigrants (PoE), who reviews the 
documents and either approves or rejects the emigration clearance, providing 
clear justifications in case of rejections.

status to reflect the outcome of the application process.

and shared with Bureau of Immigration (BOI) check posts to ensure seamless 
processing and monitoring of emigrant travel. At the airport, immigration

3.5  On the primary objectives of India’s financial aid and assistance programmes,

bilateral relations along with strengthening bonds of friendship, respect and mutual 
trust between India and partner countries underlies Indian financial aid and 
assistance programmes abroad. These reaffirm the strong ties that exist between 
India and the host country where the programmes are implemented and enhances 
India’s visibility globally, the relationship on ground with an increased people-to-
people connect and overall appreciation of the work rendered by Government of 
India. India’s approach to development is human-centric and is marked by respect, 
diversity, care for the future, and sustainable development. India's approach towards 
developmental partnerships has also been comprehensive, offering assistance while 
sharing India’s own developmental experience in the full spectrum of activities, 
ranging from creation of infrastructure to building capacities to education, healthcare, 
agriculture and community development. 
3.6  India’s aid programmes are aimed at enhancing the developmental needs of 
partner countries, which invariably makes an impact on livelihood of and socio-
economic profile of common people. Notable among them is the Government of India 
funded High Impact Community Development Projects, which are smaller in scale but 
people-oriented projects that are implemented mainly in areas of rural infrastructure 
such as drinking water supply networks, irrigation canals, farm roads, basic health 
units across social, economic and cultural sphere in friendly neighbouring countries. 
Being short gestation projects, these are delivered faster and spread across various 
parts of the recipient countries that directly impact the people at grassroots

deepening of people-to-people ties.India has also been extending several capacity

3.11  To a query of the Committee regarding the challenges faced by the Ministry in 
implementation of development partnership in other countries, the Ministry in a written reply 
has stated that implementation of large infrastructure projects is a challenging task 
irrespective of their location. The challenges are further increased when such projects are 
undertaken abroad. The nature of challenges varies from country to country depending upon 
the special circumstances under which the project is to operate. Some common issues faced 
during project execution or implementation include non-availability of encumbrance-free site, 
difficulties in land acquisition, Right of Way issues, contractual issues, delays in 
environmental impact assessments, etc. Apart from these, other major challenges include 
the changing politico-security situation in countries abroad which renders changed priority 
accorded to the project. It has been India’s endeavour to put in place a robust mechanism for 
handling all aspects of project implementation, including project formulation, appraisal, 
execution, monitoring, review and evaluation, so that challenges facing projects are 
approached in a systematic and organized manner. Priority is given to the efforts to closely 
involve and engage the host beneficiary government and other stakeholders in all aspects of 
the project to manage the challenges in nascent stage and alleviate their impact.

CHAPTER 4 
ISSUANCE OF PASSPORT 
Passport services constitute one of the most visible and citizen-centric 
functions discharged by the Ministry of External Affairs. A passport, as a document of 
national identity and sovereign guarantee, is issued under the authority of the 
Passports Act, 1967, and represents the State's formal undertaking to afford 
protection to its bearer in foreign jurisdictions. The Government of India, recognizing 
the growing demand for passport services driven by increasing outward mobility, a 
large and expanding diaspora, and rising aspirations of its citizens, has over the 
years undertaken a series of structural, technological, and administrative reforms to 
make passport issuance more accessible, transparent, and efficient. The 
establishment of the Passport Seva Programme under a Public-Private Partnership 
model marked a watershed in the delivery of passport services, transforming what 
was once a largely manual and time-consuming process into a technology-driven, 
citizen-friendly system operational across an extensive network of Passport Seva 
Kendras and Post Office Passport Seva Kendras spread throughout the country.

India maintains an extensive network of Missions and Posts abroad, 
comprising Embassies, High Commissions, Consulates General, Consulates, and 
other diplomatic offices, which together constitute the primary institutional 
mechanism through which the Government of India pursues its foreign policy 
objectives and manages its external engagements. Established under the provisions

trade, investment, and cultural ties, and provide consular and passport services to 
Indian nationals residing or travelling abroad. As on date, the Ministry of External 
Affairs administers a total of 219 Missions and Posts making India's diplomatic 
network one of the most expansive among developing nations.

PART II 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS BY THE COMMITTEE 
Overall Budgetary Allocation for 2026-27 
1. The Committee note that the Ministry of External Affairs has been 
allocated Rs. 22,118.97 crore in Budget Estimates (BE) 2026-27. This 
represents an increase of 7.81% over BE 2025-26 of Rs. 20,516.61 crore and 
1.73% over Revised Estimates (RE) 2025-26 of Rs. 21,742.74 crore. As a 
proportion of the total Union Budget 2026-27, the MEA's allocation stands at 
0.41%, which is the same as in 2025-26. The Committee observe that while the 
absolute allocation has increased in nominal terms, the proportional share has 
remained relatively low, even as India's global ambitions, diplomatic footprint, 
and development partnership commitments have expanded substantially. 
The Committee are concerned to note that the budgetary allocation for 
the Ministry of External Affairs as a percentage of the total Union Budget has 
declined consistently from 0.69% in 2017-18 to 0.41% in 2026-27. In absolute 
terms, India allocates approximately 0.06% of its GDP to foreign affairs, which 
compares unfavourably with countries such as the United States 
(approximately 0.15-0.20% of GDP) and United Kingdom (approximately 0.25-
0.30% of GDP). The Committee further note that MEA is ranked 23rd among 
Union Ministries in terms of budgetary allocation at Rs. 22,118.97 crore in BE 
2026-27, despite being entrusted with managing India's entire external 
engagement at a time when India occupies an increasingly prominent position 
in global affairs. 
In its Fifth Report on DFG 2025-26, the Committee had specifically 
recommended a budgetary enhancement of at least 20% in allocation to MEA. 
The Ministry has conveyed that this recommendation was formally 
communicated to the Ministry of Finance by the Foreign Secretary ahead of the 
pre-budget consultations. Despite this, the eventual increase has been limited 
to 7.81% - well short of what the Committee had recommended. The Committee 
are constrained to observe that this level of increase is inadequate to keep 
pace with India's expanding international engagements and the rising costs of 

187 | P a g e 
 
diplomacy. The Committee therefore, strongly recommend that due cognizance 
should to be given to the strategic imperatives driving MEA's expenditure and 
accord the Ministry a budgetary allocation commensurate with India's 
aspirations as a leading global power. The Committee reiterate their earlier 
recommendation for a budgetary enhancement of at least 20% and urge that 
the MEA's allocation be progressively raised to a level closer to the global 
benchmark for comparable major economies. The concern of the Committee 
may be conveyed to the Ministry of the Finance for further necessary action. 
 
Utilizing the RIS Report for a Stronger Case before the Ministry of Finance 
2. The Committee note that MEA currently ranks 23rd among all Ministries 
and Departments in terms of budgetary allocation, at 0.41% of the Union 
Budget. Ministries such as Finance (35.93%), Defence (14.29%), Road 
Transport and Highways (5.64%), and Railways (5.12%) understandably 
command larger shares given their domestic infrastructure mandates. 
However, the Committee are of the view that MEA's allocation must be 
compared not merely in terms of rank but in terms of the strategic multiplier it 
provides: effective diplomatic engagement secures trade, investment, 
Diaspora welfare, neighbourhood stability, and India's standing in multilateral 
institutions - dividends that accrue across sectors and are not fully captured in 
any single Ministry's budget. 
The Committee had persistently recommended that the Ministry should 
commission an independent empirical study to assess MEA's budgetary trends 
in a comparative framework. Pursuant to this recommendation, the Research 
and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) has prepared a Report 
titled 'Analysis of Trends of MEA Budgetary Allocation', examining MEA's 
budget both through an inter-Ministerial comparison within the Government of 
India and a cross-country comparison with major economies.  
The Committee recommend that MEA should utilize the RIS Report and 
update it annually with the latest figures on both inter-Ministerial allocation 
trends and cross-country comparisons. The updated Report should be 

188 | P a g e 
 
formally annexed to MEA's budget demand submission to the Ministry of 
Finance and should be shared with the Committee alongside the Demands for 
Grants. The Committee are of the view that a data-driven, rigorously 
benchmarked case before the Ministry of Finance will be far more persuasive 
than incremental administrative representations, and the RIS Report provides 
exactly the kind of credible evidence base that is required. 
 
Non-inclusion of Line of Credit Provisioning 
3. The Committee had consistently held that Line of Credit provisioning, 
which represents a notional expenditure and an adjustment of accounts 
between different branches of Government, charged to the Guaranteed 
Redemption Fund, gives a disproportionate and misleading picture of MEA's 
actual expenditure. The Committee are satisfied to note that BE 2026-27 
allocations do not include any provisioning for Lines of Credit (LoC) through 
the EXIM Bank. The Foreign Secretary, during evidence confirmed that the 
Ministry remains engaged with the Reserve Bank of India and the Ministry of 
Finance on this structural issue.  
The Committee reiterate that LoC provisioning must not be included in 
MEA's regular budget in future years. The Committee suggest that this position 
be formalized through a permanent institutional arrangement, whereby such 
provisioning is charged directly to an appropriate dedicated instrument 
managed by the Ministry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India, entirely 
outside the MEA's Demand for Grants. The Ministry should formally propose 
this structural arrangement to the concerned authorities and report back to the 
Committee on the outcome in the next year. 
 
Gap between Budgetary demand and allocation 
4. The Committee observe that there has been a persistent gap between 
the MEA’s budgetary demands and the actual allocations. In 2025-26, the 
Ministry demanded Rs. 30,871.82 crore but received only Rs. 20,516.61 crore, a 

189 | P a g e 
 
shortfall of over Rs. 10,355 crore, representing a cut of nearly 33.5% of the 
demand. In 2026-27, the Ministry demanded Rs. 25,997.56 crore and received 
Rs. 22,118.97 crore, a shortfall of Rs. 3,878.59 crore. While the Committee 
acknowledge that the gap has narrowed this year, the concern remains that 
structural underfunding needs to be addressed for continued effective 
diplomacy.  The Committee acknowledge the Ministry’s effort to rationalize its 
demands to make them more realistic and need-based. However, it is equally 
clear that even rationalized demands have been substantially cut.  
The Committee wish to make it unambiguously clear that the recurring 
demand-allocation gap is not merely an administrative inconvenience but 
represents, cumulatively, a significant underinvestment in India's diplomatic 
capacity. As India aspires to play a leading role in global governance, 
multilateral institutions, regional connectivity, and the Global South, the 
financial resources made available to the Ministry of External Affairs must 
reflect that ambition. The Committee recommend that the Ministry should 
accompany each Budget demand with a detailed, head-wise justification note, 
supported by empirical data and outcome metrics, to enable the Ministry of 
Finance to make a fully informed appraisal. The RIS Report and cross-country 
benchmarks should be integral parts of this justification. The Committee 
further recommend that the Ministry should institutionalize a structured pre-
budget dialogue with the Ministry of Finance before the preparation of the 
Union Budget. The Committee also urge the Ministry of Finance to undertake a 
more rigorous and sympathetic appraisal of MEA's budgetary demands, which 
are driven by national interests, externally determined factors such as foreign 
exchange fluctuations, opening of new Missions and Posts, and India's 
expanding development assistance portfolio etc.

7. Under the Scheme/Non-Scheme classification, ‘Scheme’ expenditure, 
comprising India’s development assistance and technical and economic 
cooperation programmes, stands at Rs. 6,997.56 crore in BE 2026-27, while

stands at Rs. 15,121.41 crore. The Committee note with concern that the

classification is not MEA-specific but has been determined by the Ministry of

expenditure given their socio-economic outcomes in partner countries. 
The Committee emphasize that development assistance is not merely a 
budgetary outlay but is the most visible and consequential instrument of 
India’s bilateral diplomacy, particularly in the neighbourhood, the Global 
South, Africa, and the Indo-Pacific. Reductions in scheme allocations, even if 
driven by legitimate bilateral considerations, risk signaling a withdrawal of 
India’s developmental engagement to partner countries and can erode 
goodwill built over years of sustained investment. The Committee are also 
concerned to note that there is no budgetary mechanism to protect the

development assistance to other partner countries or for new development

Southeast Asia from exploitation, trafficking, and illegal recruitment. However, 
the Committee are concerned that the total budget for the PGE is entirely 
disproportionate to the scale and complexity of the responsibilities involved. 
The Committee are particularly concerned that the budget for public 
awareness campaigns to inform emigrants of their rights stands at a mere Rs. 
73 lakh in 2025-26. The Committee also note that with only 16 PoE offices in a 
country of 28 states and 8 Union Territories, there is a need to establish PoE 
offices in other parts of our country, including major emigration source states, 
that have no local PoE presence. 
The Committee recommend that the Ministry should undertake an urgent 
and comprehensive review of the budgetary requirements of the PGoE and the 
PoE network, and make enhanced allocations to levels commensurate with the 
scale and sensitivity of the responsibilities involved. The Committee further 
recommend that the Ministry should prepare a phased PoE Network Expansion 
Plan, identifying States with the highest ECR emigrant populations but no PoE 
presence, estimating the cost of establishing new offices in these States, and 
setting a time-bound schedule for expansion, beginning with the completion of 
pending offices in Vijayawada (Andhra Pradesh) and the approved one in 
Madhya Pradesh. It is also essential that these offices are located in accessible

Combating Illegal Recruitment 
15. The Committee note that despite the eMigrate portal, the mPassport 
Police App, and the network of PoE offices, illegal recruitment agencies and 
unauthorized intermediaries continue to operate, exploiting vulnerable Indian 
workers seeking employment abroad. The Committee observe that the Ministry 
has acknowledged the challenge of combating fraud in the recruitment 
process and the need for coordination with local police and cyber-crime units, 
but has not provided the Committee with specific data on the scale of illegal 
recruitment activity, the number of agents prosecuted, or the outcomes of 
enforcement actions. The Committee are of the firm view that the protection of 
Indian workers from exploitation, trafficking, and fraudulent recruitment is a 
fundamental obligation of the State, and that the current enforcement 
architecture - characterized by a small PoE network, limited financial 
resources, and dependence on State police coordination - appear insufficient 
to meet this obligation at the required scale. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that MEA should develop and 
implement, in coordination with concerned Ministries (such as Home Affairs 
and Labour and Employment) and state governments, a comprehensive 
strategy to counter illegal recruitment, encompassing a strengthened 
regulatory framework for recruiting agents, enhanced digital monitoring of 
online recruitment advertising, coordination with social media platforms to 
detect and remove fraudulent job advertisements, and a dedicated rapid 
response mechanism for distress cases involving illegal recruitment. The 
Committee further recommend that the Ministry institute a publicly accessible, 
real-time blacklisted illegal and deregistered recruiting agents, accessible to 
potential emigrants and their families through the eMigrate portal, MADAD, and 
other citizen-centric platforms and also work with State governments to ensure

that local police are aware of and act against the blacklisted agents operating 
in their jurisdictions. 
New Emigration Bill 
16. The emigration framework in India is governed by the Emigration Act, 
1983, administered by MEA through the Protector General of Emigrants. In the 
four decades since its enactment, India’s outward labour migration has grown 
exponentially in scale, complexity, and vulnerability. The Committee have in 
previous reports persistently called for the introduction of a comprehensive 
new Emigration Bill. The Ministry has in successive responses acknowledged 
the preparation of the draft Bill and stated that it is under ‘active 
consideration.’ In pursuance of the Committee’s recommendation contained in 
Sixth Report, the Ministry provided the draft Overseas Mobility (Facilitation and 
Welfare) Bill, 2025 to the Committee and sought feedback from Committee 
Members. The feedback was sent to the Ministry in December 2025. The 
Committee note that the introduction of the new Bill has remained pending 
despite the completion of the Committee’s feedback, and reiterate that the 
matter deserves to be treated as a legislative priority. The Committee strongly 
recommend that the Government treat the introduction of the Overseas 
Mobility (Facilitation and Welfare) Bill, 2025 as a legislative priority and 
introduce it in Parliament at the earliest opportunity. The Committee are 
hopeful that once introduced, the Bill will be referred to it for detailed 
examination, in view of its significance and wider implications.

vulnerable to deterioration in the quality of its academic offering, which would 
defeat the very purpose for which SAU was established. The Committee 
recommend that the Ministry should identify and pursue specific steps, within 
the existing governance framework, to strengthen SAU’s academic profile and 
international visibility, including by facilitating research partnerships with 
Indian universities and research institutions, extending SAARC Silver Jubilee 
Scholarships to a wider cohort of students, and supporting SAU’s participation 
in regional academic networks and knowledge-exchange platforms. SAU’s 
potential as a symbol of India’s commitment to regional integration and as a 
platform for people-to-people connectivity within South Asia can only be 
realized if the institution is demonstrably well-resourced, well-managed, and 
academically credible. 
 
 
 

229 | P a g e 
 
Assistance to autonomous bodies and institutions 
57. The Committee note that the Ministry of External Affairs provides 
Grants-in-Aid to autonomous bodies and institutions, principally the Indian 
Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), the Indian Council of World Affairs 
(ICWA), and the Research and Information System for Developing Countries 
(RIS).  These institutions are not administrative extensions of the Ministry but 
are the intellectual and cultural infrastructure through which India’s diplomacy 
acquires depth, reach, and the capacity to engage the world beyond the formal. 
The total allocation to these institutions has grown from Rs. 369.85 crore in BE 
2024-25 to Rs. 451.19 crore in BE 2026-27. The Committee note that the 
Ministry has put in place an established accountability framework for these 
institutions.  
The Committee observe that while the budgetary allocation for this head 
has grown incrementally, the Committee are of the view that the increase is 
modest relative to the scale of India’s foreign policy objectives. Further, there 
is a lack of structured and outcome-oriented framework that links the research 
mandates of these institutions to the Ministry’s identified foreign policy 
priorities. The Committee urge the Ministry to establish a formal, structured 
mechanism for integrating the research outputs of ICWA and RIS into MEA’s 
foreign policy formulation process. The Committee further recommend that the 
Ministry, in coordination with ICCR, ICWA, and RIS, should develop a 
coordinated global outreach strategy that identifies countries of priority 
strategic importance, where the combined intellectual and cultural presence of 
India’s autonomous bodies will be systematically strengthened. 
 
Budgetary Allocation to Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR) 
58.  The Committee acknowledge that Indian Council for Cultural Relations 
(ICCR) plays a pivotal role in projecting India’s soft power and advancing its 
cultural diplomacy through a wide spectrum of activities such as scholarships, 
cultural delegations, Indian Cultural Centres abroad, promotion of Indian 
languages, performing arts, and the International Day of Yoga. The Committee 

230 | P a g e 
 
note that the budgetary allocation for ICCR has been enhanced from Rs. 351.25 
crore in BE 2025-26 to Rs. 391.50 crore in BE 2026-27. However, ICCR had 
sought Rs. 410.21 crore for BE 2026-27, leaving a gap of Rs. 18.71 crore 
between the institution’s assessed requirement and the allocation made. The 
Ministry has stated that this enhanced allocation will support an expanded 
scholarship intake, a larger number of outgoing and incoming cultural 
delegations, the International Day of Yoga 2026, additional ICCR Chairs, and 
increased activities at Indian Cultural Centres.  The Committee further note 
that ICCR has virtually no independent revenue base. Its own earnings from 
auditorium and art gallery rentals amounted to only Rs. 95.43 lakh in 2024-25, 
making it almost wholly dependent on the Ministry’s grant for all its activities. 
The Ministry has itself acknowledged, in its reply to this Committee, that ICCR 
would need more budgetary allocations and resources to discharge its 
mandate fully. 
Keeping in view the broad and expanding mandate of ICCR as a frontline 
instrument of India’s soft power, the Committee are of the considered opinion 
that the current level of budgetary support needs to be suitably enhanced. The 
Committee have previously observed that ICCR’s allocation has historically 
remained in the range of Rs. 300-350 crore annually, and while the 
enhancement to Rs. 391.50 crore in BE 2026-27 is a welcome step, the 
Committee contend that such funding levels remain insufficient relative to the 
scale, ambition, and expanding scope of ICCR’s activities. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly reiterate their recommendation that ICCR’s budgetary 
allocation be raised to Rs. 500-600 crore in the forthcoming years, in a phased 
and planned manner, to enable ICCR to discharge its pivotal mandate of 
cultural outreach, educational diplomacy, and promotion of India’s soft power 
with the scale and quality that India’s rising global profile demands. In the 
immediate term, the Committee recommend that the Ministry address the 
unfunded gap of Rs. 18.71 crore at the Revised Estimates stage of 2026-27 so 
that ICCR’s expanded programme commitments are not curtailed. 
 
 
 

231 | P a g e 
 
ICCR Scholarships 
59. The Committee note that the ICCR scholarship programme, with 3,649 
students availing scholarships in 2025-26 under 21 schemes, is one of India’s 
most enduring and cost-effective soft power instruments. The current Prime 
Minister of Sri Lanka and the High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to India are both 
ICCR alumni, an illustration of the long-term diplomatic returns that the 
programme generates. The Committee endorse the Ministry’s stated intent to 
enhance total scholarship slots in academic year 2026-27 and urge that this 
expansion be accompanied by a strategic review of slot allocation across 
countries, with deliberate effort to expand reach into the Indo-Pacific, West 
Asia, Central Asia, and Latin America, where India’s strategic footprint is 
growing but ICCR’s scholarship presence remains limited. The Committee also 
recommend that ICCR strengthen its alumni engagement programme and 
maintain active networks with former scholarship holders, given the 
demonstrable diplomatic returns that well-connected alumni deliver. 
ICCR Cultural Centres 
 
60. The Committee are aware that the 38 Indian Cultural Centres (ICCs) 
serve as vital instruments in projecting India’s rich and diverse cultural 
heritage through a wide array of activities, including dance, music, yoga, 
languages, food, festivals, history, and contemporary cultural narratives. The 
Committee note that ICCR and MEA are in the process of reviewing the 
locations of India’s 38 Indian Cultural Centres abroad, with a view to opening 
new Centres in strategically important countries and ensuring that existing 
Centres are located where they can have the greatest impact.  
The previous DFG reports of the Committee had called for expedited 
operationalization of the Indian Cultural Centres in Washington DC and Paris. 
The Committee welcome the completion of renovation at the Swami 
Vivekananda Cultural Centre in Paris. The Committee are, however, deeply 
concerned that the Washington DC property, located in the capital of one of 
India’s most strategically significant bilateral partner, is now being 
recommended for sale on the basis of a 2024 Property Management Team 
assessment, without any clear alternative arrangement. The Committee place 
on record that USD 4,41,581.91 has already been expended on consultancy 
services for this property, that the United States hosts one of the world’s 
largest and most influential Indian diaspora communities, and that the absence 
of a dedicated ICCR Cultural Centre in Washington DC may represent a 
significant and conspicuous gap in India’s cultural diplomacy infrastructure. 
The Committee urge the Ministry to take necessary steps for providing 
institutional presence in Washington, United States and inform the Committee 
about it. 
Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA) 

232 | P a g e 
 
61. The Committee note that the Indian Council of World Affairs, established 
in 1943 and accorded statutory status under the Indian Council of World 
Affairs Act, 2001, is one of India’s oldest and most distinguished institutions 
for research and dialogue on foreign policy. While the budgetary allocation of 
ICWA has witnessed an upward trend from Rs. 15.48 crore in BE 2025-26 to Rs. 
28.88 crore in BE 2026-27, the Committee observe the increase is primarily 
attributed to salaries ad capital expenditure. The Committee note that ICWA 
has been highly productive in recent years. in 2025 alone, the Council 
published 180 research papers, 12 special publications by eminent external 
scholars, and 9 books.  The Committee observe that ICWA’s schedule of 
bilateral and multilateral dialogues for 2026-27 is extensive, covering 17 
bilateral and multilateral engagements across Asia, Europe, Latin America, and 
the Gulf. The Committee observe that this level of convening activity 
represents a significant and strategically valuable contribution to India’s 
foreign policy ecosystem, and recommend that the Ministry ensure that 
ICWA’s programme commitments under its 2026-27 calendar are fully funded 
and that any supplementary programme requirements arising from ICWA’s 
chairship responsibilities are anticipated and provided for at the RE stage. At 
the same time, the Committee express grave concern at the failure to convene 
even a single Governing Council meeting, which raise great concern about its 
accountability.  
Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) 
62. The Committee note that the Research and Information System for 
Developing Countries, established in 1983 under the Ministry of External 
Affairs, is a policy research institution of considerable standing whose work 
on trade, development cooperation, connectivity, South-South cooperation, 
and science diplomacy strengthen India’s positions at the WTO, BRICS, 
BIMSTEC, ASEAN, and other multilateral forums. The Committee note that 
RIS’s allocation has been increased from Rs. 19.51 crore in BE 2025-26 to Rs. 
24.87 crore in BE 2026-27, an increase of Rs. 5.36 crore, driven by India’s 
Chairship of BRICS and IORA and associated expanded programmatic 
commitments. RIS currently collaborates with approximately 351 institutions 
worldwide, 79 within India and 272 internationally. RIS has also established a 

233 | P a g e 
 
significant institutional infrastructure: DAKSHIN  (the Global South Centre of 
Excellence) was created at RIS with Government support; the ASEAN-India 
Centre supports Act East policy research; the Centre for Maritime Economy 
and Connectivity (CMEC) was established with Indian Ports Association 
support; and a new Natural Resources vertical is being introduced in FY 2026-
27, reflecting the growing strategic importance of critical minerals and energy 
security within India’s trade and geopolitical framework. 
The Committee are of the view that RIS’s eight thematic centres and its 
wide-ranging activities represent a formidable institutional architecture for 
multilateral engagement that is substantially underfunded relative to its 
potential. The Committee, therefore, advise the Ministry to conduct a 
systematic review of the resource requirements of RIS, with a view to 
providing dedicated and predictable funding.

(Recommendation No. 1) 
India's Strategic Responsibility in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) 
5. The Committee in their report has observed/recommended as under: 
“The Committee acknowledge the paramount strategic, economic, and 
environmental significance of the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) for India. With a 
coastline of over 7,500 kilometres, coupled with its vast Exclusive Economic 
Zone (EEZ) of 2.4 million square kilometres, India is uniquely positioned at the 
heart of one of the most vital regions in the world. Nearly 90% of India's trade 
by volume, including oil imports, transits through the Indian Ocean which also 
handles half of the world's container shipments. Thus, the Indian Ocean is not 
only critical for India's economic stability but also serves as a bridge for global 
trade between Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. 
Given this geo-strategic importance, the Committee are of the considered 
view that India's leadership role in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) is both a 
natural and necessary extension of its geopolitical and economic interests and 
thereby, it should take a leading role in ensuring the security, stability, and 
prosperity of the region. The Committee observe that India's leadership in the 
Indian Ocean is underscored by its strategic framework, Vision SAGAR 
(Security and Growth for All in the Region) and its evolved version, Vision 
MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth 
Across Regions for the Global South). These guiding principles accentuate 
India's commitment to a rules-based order, respect for sovereignty, freedom 
of navigation, and the protection of regional maritime security. The Indian 
Ocean is undeniably an integral part of India's global strategy, and it is in 
India's best interest to assert its role as a guardian of this vital maritime space. 
The Committee urge that the MEA should intensify its efforts to build stronger 
bilateral, multilateral engagements and defence partnerships while ensuring 
the region's sustainability and security. By fostering a cooperative, rules-
based order in the Indian Ocean, India should continue enhancing its role as a 
leading regional power, securing the region for itself and the global 
community, while affirming that the Indian Ocean remains India's Ocean.” 
 

3 | P a g e 
 
6. In its action-taken reply, the Ministry of External Affairs has stated as under: 
“As demonstrated by frequent high level visits and the outcomes thereof, India 
continues to strengthen bilateral engagements in the region. India is 
committed to further strengthening defence and security cooperation in the 
region through continued provision of military assets, joint exercises, high 
level bilateral visits as well as capacity building support. Conclusion of MoU 
on Defence Cooperation with Sri Lanka, construction of Maldives National 
Defence Forces Coast Guard Harbour, enhanced strategic partnership with 
Mauritius, signing of Charter and MoU for establishment of the Colombo 
Security Conclave, regular joint exercises with defence forces, provisioning of 
defence security platforms, training and capacity building, are some of the 
recent measures that reaffirm our intent for closer cooperation in the security 
and defence domains aimed at tackling common security challenges in the 
region.”     
7. Acknowledging the paramount strategic, economic, and environmental 
significance of the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) for India, the Committee in their 
original Report had urged the MEA to intensify its efforts to build stronger 
bilateral, multilateral engagements and defence partnerships to ensure 
region’s sustainability and security.  The Committee note from the Action 
Taken Reply furnished by the Ministry that India is committed to further 
strengthening defence and security cooperation in the region through 
continued provision of military assets, joint exercises, high level bilateral 
visits as well as capacity building support.  Some of the recent measures 
taken in this regard are conclusion of MoU on Defence Cooperation with Sri 
Lanka, construction of Maldives National Defence Forces Coast Guard 
Harbour, enhanced strategic partnership with Mauritius, signing of Charter and 
MoU for establishment of the Colombo Security Conclave, regular joint 
exercises with defence forces, provisioning of defence security platforms, 
training and capacity building, etc.  The Committee are of the view that Indian 
Ocean is undeniably an integral part of India’s global strategy. The importance 
of the Indian Ocean Region can be seen from the fact that it is spread over an 
area of over 70 million square kilometers, connecting over 35 littoral states 
and is home to one third of the world’s population.  India also has a significant 
stake in the Indian Ocean Region, with coastline exceeding 11,098 kilometers 
and India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) spanning 2.4 million square 
kilometers, and handles 90 per cent of India’s trade volume.  Globally, these 
waters handle half of container shipments, a third of bulk cargo, and two thirds 

4 | P a g e 
 
of oil shipments.  Considering that Indian Ocean is vital not only to India’s 
geopolitical, economic and cultural landscape, but also for maintaining 
regional and global order, the Committee desire that a more comprehensive 
strategy which will adequately enable India to take a leading role in ensuring 
security, stability and prosperity in the region may be worked out by the 
Ministry.  The Committee has noted some of the recent initiatives taken by the 
Government to address the security and various other concerns in the Indian 
Ocean Region.  The Committee are of the view that more initiatives are 
required to enable India to take a leading role in the region In view of this, the 
Committee once again urge the Ministry of External Affairs to take further 
necessary measures to deepen bilateral, multilateral engagements, expand 
defence partnerships, and formulate a comprehensive regional strategy that 
will adequately reflects the centrality of the Indian Ocean in India’s long-term 
strategic outlook. 
 
(Recommendation No.9) 
Countering Chinese Expansion and Influence in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) 
 
8. The Committee in their report had observed/recommended as under: 
“The Committee express concern regarding the escalating Chinese presence 
and its increasing influence in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR), a development 
which poses substantial risks to India's national security and broader strategic 
interests. The Committee recognizes that China's enhanced naval 
capabilities, exemplified by the growing size of its fleet, including over 15 units 
commissioned annually, has now surpassed the United States Navy, making 
it the world's largest naval force. The induction of advanced warships, 
including multiple Carrier Battle Groups and an additional aircraft carrier, 
along with the regular deployment of Chinese submarines and naval vessels, 
demonstrates a clear and growing strategic interest by China in consolidating 
its position in the IOR.  
The strategic positioning of Chinese military and commercial infrastructure 
across key maritime chokepoints, particularly under the Belt and Road 
Initiative (BRI) and the "String of Pearls" strategy, is gradually reconfiguring 
the region's geopolitical dynamics in favor of Chinese interests. Of equal 
concern is the strengthening of the China-Pakistan naval nexus, which not 
only facilitates joint military exercises but also advances Pakistan's naval 
modernization. This cooperation complicates the security situation further, 
particularly in the context of the increasing Chinese influence over Pakistan's 
naval assets, which could destabilize the balance of power in the region. 

5 | P a g e 
 
The Committee believe that these developments must be addressed with 
urgency, as they have the potential to shift the balance of power in the region, 
challenging India's strategic autonomy and undermining its influence over key 
maritime chokepoints. In the considered view of the Committee, India must 
remain proactive in countering the combined naval threat from China and 
Pakistan by bolstering its own deterrence capabilities and conducting joint 
exercises with partner countries to maintain strategic balance. The Committee 
urge the Government to enhance Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) through 
further integration of advanced technologies, such as satellite-based 
surveillance systems and Artificial Intelligence, to monitor Chinese activities 
more effectively. This should be complemented by a significant upgradation in 
naval capabilities, including the induction of advanced anti-submarine warfare 
(ASW) vessels, surveillance aircrafts, and nuclear-powered submarines, 
ensuring India's readiness to respond to any emerging threat. India should 
also deepen its strategic alliances with regional powers and global partners, 
particularly through forums such as the Quad, to ensure collective security 
and strengthen deterrence. Building closer ties with IOR littoral states through 
defense cooperation, capacity-building initiatives, and joint maritime 
operations will be crucial in countering Chinese influence.” 
9. In its action-taken reply, the Ministry of External Affairs has stated as under: 
“The Indian Navy is seized of the security implications of the combined naval 
threat from China and Pakistan, and maintains a constant and close watch on 
their deployments. The Indian Navy concept of operations are being 
continuously fine-tuned and capability perspective plans are being pursued to 
counter all emerging threats. The commissioning of INS Vikrant, and the 
continued modernization of our submarine fleet, including nuclear-powered 
submarines is aimed at ensuring that we retain a credible deterrence in the 
region. The Navy’s anti-submarine warfare capabilities have also been 
significantly enhanced with induction of ASW corvettes, P8I Long Range 
Maritime Reconnaissance aircraft and the MH-60R helicopters. Whole of 
Government efforts are also being pursued to augment underwater domain 
awareness (UDA) in the region. 
Indian Navy has enhanced strategic partnerships through increased 
deployments, joint exercises and collaborations with like-minded navies in the 
region. Partnerships through bilateral and multilateral exercises like the Rim of 
the Pacific Exercise (RIMPAC), Malabar, Varuna, Konkan and initiatives like

Recommendation No. 2

security interests. The increasing militarization of ports, alongside activities

situation. Additionally, issues like climate change, marine pollution, and the 
destruction of marine biodiversity threaten the ecological balance of the 
region and, in turn, regional food security and disaster resilience.

adopt a multifaceted and comprehensive approach to securing and stabilizing 
the Indian Ocean. As the largest and most influential nation in the Indian 
Ocean Region, India is uniquely positioned to act as the net security provider.

regional stability, ensuring maritime security, and safeguarding the interests

countries that face infrastructural and financial constraints.

engagement beyond the IOR to the entire Global South, including Africa. At

about the outcome of its assessment within three months.

only critical for India's economic stability but also serves as a bridge for global

accentuate India's commitment to a rules-based order, respect for sovereignty, 
freedom of navigation, and the protection of regional maritime security. The

in India's best interest to assert its role as a guardian of this vital maritime 
space. The Committee urge that the MEA should intensify its efforts to build 
stronger bilateral, multilateral engagements and defence partnerships while 
ensuring the region's sustainability and security. By fostering a cooperative, 
rules-based order in the Indian Ocean, India should continue enhancing its

community, while affirming that the Indian Ocean remains India's Ocean.
